items.title: Reintroducing wolves changed the course of rivers in Yellowstone
items.claim: Grey wolves were exterminated from Yellowstone by 1926. In 1995, 14 wolves were reintroduced. Within 20 years, elk populations dropped, willows and aspen regrew along riverbanks, beaver populations rose, and river channels narrowed.

options.text: A trophic cascade: wolves reduce elk numbers and (especially) keep them moving, releasing browse pressure on streamside trees, which stabilise banks. The effect propagates through multiple trophic levels
Wolves drink large amounts of river water
It's coincidence — climate change did it

items.reveal:
The Yellowstone story is the textbook trophic cascade. Wolves don't only kill elk; they shift elk behaviour — herds avoid areas where they can't see predators coming, like valley bottoms with dense vegetation.

Released from constant browsing, willows and aspens regrow. Beavers, which need willows, return — by 2014, beaver colonies had increased from 1 to 9. Beaver dams trap sediment, raise water tables, create wetlands.

The full claim ('wolves changed the rivers') is contested. William Ripple and Robert Beschta documented the vegetation rebound; Arthur Middleton and others argue confounding factors (climate, bear predation, elk hunting outside the park) explain much of it.

What is uncontroversial: keystone species have effects on ecosystems vastly out of proportion to their biomass. Sea otters and kelp forests, starfish and intertidal communities, sharks and seagrass — similar cascades documented worldwide.

Keystone species concept: Robert Paine (1969), who removed starfish from a Pacific Northwest tide pool and watched it collapse to a mussel monoculture.
items.why: Ecosystems are imagined as bottom-up: plants determine herbivores determine carnivores. Top predators flip the picture — top-down control is real, and big effects can come from species with little biomass.

items.title: Species are vanishing 100 to 1000 times faster than normal
items.claim: The fossil record gives a 'background' extinction rate: roughly 1 species per million per year. Current rates are 100 to 1000 times that — and rising. Many biologists call it the sixth mass extinction.

options.text: Asteroid impact like 66 million years ago
Habitat destruction (especially tropical deforestation), invasive species, climate change, pollution and overharvesting — a multi-cause anthropogenic mass extinction with no single dominant mechanism

items.reveal:
The five previous mass extinctions (Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous) each saw 50-95% of species disappear over geological timescales. The Permian was the worst — ~96% of marine species lost over ~60,000 years.

The current rate, calculated from documented vertebrate extinctions (Ceballos, Ehrlich and others), is 100-1000 times background. Insect biomass declines (Hallmann et al. 2017, Krefeld study) show 75% reductions over 27 years in German nature reserves.

Human impacts: forest cover reduced by ~30% globally since 1700; ocean fish biomass down ~50% since 1970; freshwater vertebrates down 84% (WWF Living Planet Report). Climate change adds an accelerating layer.

Protected areas and conservation work — by some measures, extinction rates would have been 4x higher without them.

Mass extinctions reshape evolution for tens of millions of years. We won't return to the world we know within human-relevant timeframes — the species we lose are lost.
items.why: Species loss feels gradual. The rate is geological in magnitude — comparable to events that left fossil-record-defining boundaries. We are living through one.

items.title: Trees in a forest can be physically connected to each other through fungi
items.claim: Most plant roots are colonised by mycorrhizal fungi. Filaments (hyphae) extend from one tree's root system through the soil to other trees, exchanging carbon, nutrients and chemical signals. The network has been called the 'wood wide web'.
items.prompt: What does the fungal network do?

options.text: Mycorrhizal fungi exchange phosphorus and water for sugars with plant roots; the same fungal network often connects multiple trees, and there's evidence that carbon can flow from one tree to another along this network
Fungi feed only on dead plants
Trees connect to other trees directly without fungi

items.reveal:
About 80-90% of land plant species form mycorrhizal associations:
- Arbuscular mycorrhizae (AMF, Glomeromycota): hyphae penetrate root cells. Common in grasses, most flowering plants. Ancient (~400 million years, possibly enabled land plants to colonise dry land).
- Ectomycorrhizae (basidiomycetes and ascomycetes): hyphae form a sheath around roots and grow between cells. Common in temperate and boreal trees (pine, oak, birch).

The fungi gain sugars from the plant; the plant gains greatly expanded effective root surface area for nutrient and water absorption.

Networks: ectomycorrhizal fungi often colonise multiple trees with a continuous mycelium. Suzanne Simard's experiments (1997 Nature, follow-ups) used isotope-labelled carbon to show carbon flow between Douglas firs and paper birches via fungal connections.

The 'mother tree' hypothesis (Simard, popularised) is controversial — the magnitude and direction of carbon flow, and whether it represents 'communication' rather than diffusion, is still debated. Some recent reviews argue effects are smaller and less directional than originally claimed.

What's not in doubt: mycorrhizal networks are real, sometimes vast (one Armillaria fungus in Oregon covers 9.7 km^2 and is ~2400 years old), and important for nutrient cycling, drought tolerance and forest dynamics.

Agriculture is starting to take mycorrhizae seriously — many fertilizer regimes inadvertently suppress them, reducing long-term soil health.
items.why: Trees look like independent giants. Under the soil they are nodes in fungal networks — sharing nutrients, sometimes carbon, and almost certainly signals. The unit of life is harder to define than it looks.
